questions.q: Define a sigma (σ) bond and a pi (π) bond in terms of orbital overlap geometry. Which type of overlap (s-s, s-p, p-p axial, p-p lateral) produces each bond type?
questions.a: A sigma (σ) bond forms by end-to-end (axial) overlap of orbitals along the internuclear axis (s-s, s-p, or p-p axial). A pi (π) bond forms by sidewise (lateral) overlap where orbital axes are parallel and perpendicular to the internuclear axis (p-p lateral only). A wrong answer (e.g., saying π bonds form from s-p overlap) reveals the student confuses orbital types with overlap geometry - they haven't grasped that π bonds require parallel p-orbitals with sidewise overlap, while σ bonds can form from any axial combination.

questions.q: Two hydrogen atoms approach each other. At infinite separation, potential energy is zero. As they approach, potential energy decreases to a minimum of -435.8 kJ/mol at 74 pm, then rises sharply. Explain why energy first decreases then increases, referencing attractive and repulsive forces.
questions.a: Initially, nucleus-electron attraction (cross-attraction between nucleus A and electron B, nucleus B and electron A) dominates over electron-electron and nucleus-nucleus repulsion, lowering energy. At 74 pm, net force is zero (minimum energy). Closer than 74 pm, nucleus-nucleus and electron-electron repulsion increase sharply, raising energy. A wrong answer (e.g., "energy keeps decreasing" or "only attraction matters") shows the student misses the balance of four forces and the physical meaning of bond distance as equilibrium point.

questions.q: In the formation of HCl molecule, the half-filled 1s orbital of H overlaps with the half-filled 3p_z orbital of Cl along the internuclear axis (taken as z-axis). Identify the bond type formed and predict whether the overlap is positive, negative, or zero if the 3p_z orbital's positive lobe overlaps with the 1s orbital.
questions.a: The bond formed is a sigma (σ) bond (s-p axial overlap). Since the 1s orbital is spherically symmetric (always positive) and the 3p_z positive lobe has the same phase/sign, the overlap is positive, leading to bond formation. A wrong answer (e.g., "π bond" or "negative overlap") reveals confusion between σ/π classification and overlap sign conventions - the student may not understand that σ/π depends on geometry (axial vs lateral), while positive/negative/zero overlap depends on phase matching.

questions.q: Compare the expected bond angles in CH₄ if carbon used pure atomic orbitals (2s, 2p_x, 2p_y, 2p_z) for bonding versus the actual tetrahedral angle of 109.5°. Why does simple orbital overlap theory fail to predict the correct geometry?
questions.a: With pure orbitals: three C-H bonds from 2p orbitals would be at 90° to each other (p_x, p_y, p_z mutually perpendicular), and the 2s orbital is spherically symmetric (no preferred direction). Actual CH₄ has four equivalent C-H bonds at 109.5°. Simple overlap fails because it doesn't account for equivalent hybrid orbitals that minimize electron pair repulsion (VSEPR). A wrong answer (e.g., "2s orbital gives 90° too" or "VSEPR not related") shows the student hasn't connected VB theory's limitation to the need for hybridisation and VSEPR concepts from c11_chem_cbse_04_005.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "A double bond consists of two π bonds because π bonds are formed by sidewise overlap which allows more electron sharing." Is it correct? Justify using bond strength and overlap extent.
questions.a: Incorrect. A double bond consists of one σ bond (axial overlap, greater extent, stronger) and one π bond (lateral overlap, smaller extent, weaker). σ bonds are stronger because axial overlap has greater orbital interpenetration than lateral overlap. The statement reverses the bond composition and misattributes strength to π bonds. A wrong evaluation reveals the student confuses bond multiplicity with bond type strength and doesn't understand overlap extent determines bond energy.

questions.q: Design a conceptual experiment using diatomic molecules H₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂ to demonstrate the relationship between orbital overlap extent, bond length, and bond dissociation enthalpy. What trend would you expect and why?
questions.a: Measure bond lengths (spectroscopy) and bond dissociation enthalpies for H₂ (74 pm, 436 kJ/mol), F₂ (144 pm, 159 kJ/mol), Cl₂ (199 pm, 242 kJ/mol), Br₂ (228 pm, 193 kJ/mol), I₂ (267 pm, 151 kJ/mol). Trend: as atomic size increases down group, orbital overlap extent decreases → bond length increases → bond enthalpy generally decreases (except F₂ anomaly due to lone pair repulsion). A poor answer (no trend, wrong direction, ignores F₂ anomaly) shows the student can't connect atomic size → overlap extent → macroscopic properties.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Valence Bond Theory explains covalent bond formation through the overlap of half-filled atomic orbitals ______ electrons with opposite spins, resulting in electron pairing and increased electron density between nuclei.
Fill in the blank: When two ______ atoms approach each other, you can observe that they form a stable H₂ molecule with bond length 74 pm and bond energy 435.8 kJ/mol.
Fill in the blank: Begin by asking: why do two separate H atoms (each with ______s¹ electron) release energy when they combine?
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can predict bond type (σ/π) and relative bond strength from given orbital overlap diagrams, explain why simple atomic orbital overlap fails to predict molecular geometries (e.g., CH₄ tetrahedral angle 109.5° vs 90° from p-orbitals), and calculate bond order from σ/π bond count in diatomic and polyatomic molecules.
